families.label: Common Roots
families.blurb: The one stream every branch below flows from: Israel, Jesus and the apostles, the early church, and the great councils that confessed the faith.

families.label: Church of the East
families.blurb: The ancient church of Persia and Asia, separated after the Council of Ephesus (431); its missionaries reached India and China centuries before the West did.

families.label: Oriental Orthodox
families.blurb: The churches of Egypt, Syria, Armenia, Ethiopia and India that did not accept the Council of Chalcedon (451) — among the oldest continuous churches on earth.

families.label: Eastern Orthodox
families.blurb: The Chalcedonian churches of the Greek East — Constantinople, the Slavic lands and beyond — formally separated from Rome in the Great Schism of 1054.

families.label: Catholic
families.blurb: The Western church in communion with the bishop of Rome — by far the largest single Christian body, present in nearly every nation.

families.label: Reformation Forerunners
families.blurb: Medieval movements that reached for Scripture in the people's language and a simpler church — a century and more before Luther.

families.label: Lutheran
families.blurb: The churches that grew from Martin Luther's recovery of justification by faith alone — Germany, Scandinavia, and their daughter churches worldwide.

families.label: Reformed & Presbyterian
families.blurb: The Swiss stream of the Reformation — Zwingli, Calvin, Knox — spreading through the Netherlands, Scotland, France, and the Puritans to the wider world.

families.label: Anglican
families.blurb: The Church of England and its global communion — reformed in doctrine, ancient in structure, a via media that later birthed Methodism and much else.

families.label: Anabaptists & Free Churches
families.blurb: The 'radical reformation' and the free-church dissenters: believers' baptism, gathered churches, simplicity and peace — Mennonites, Amish, Brethren, Quakers.

families.label: Baptist
families.blurb: Churches of baptized believers, congregationally governed — born among English separatists in 1609 and now one of the largest Protestant families.

families.label: Methodist & Holiness
families.blurb: The Wesleyan revival inside the Church of England became a worldwide family — and its holiness stream later kindled Pentecostalism.

families.label: Restorationist & Adventist
families.blurb: American movements that set out to restore New Testament Christianity — the Stone-Campbell churches, the Brethren, and the Adventist stream.

families.label: Pentecostal & Charismatic
families.blurb: The 20th century's great renewal of the Spirit's gifts — from Azusa Street to the charismatic movement and today's global church-planting families.

families.label: African-Initiated
families.blurb: Churches founded by African leaders on African soil — from the Zionist and Apostolic movements to some of the largest congregations in the world.

families.label: Non-Nicene Groups
families.blurb: Groups that grew out of Christian history but do not confess the Nicene faith in the Trinity — shown for the sake of the map, and badged clearly.

families.label: Early Divisions
families.blurb: The movements the early church tested and did not receive — Gnostic teachers, Marcion, the New Prophecy, Arius, the Donatists. None survives as a church today, but the answers they forced are why we have a creed, a canon and a doctrine of the church at all.

nodes.name: Ancient Israel
nodes.blurb: God calls Abraham and covenants with his family — the people through whom the Messiah comes and the Scriptures are given.

nodes.name: Second Temple Judaism
nodes.blurb: After the exile the Temple is rebuilt; synagogues, scribes, Pharisees and Sadducees shape the world Jesus is born into.

nodes.name: Jesus & the Apostles
nodes.blurb: The life, death and resurrection of Jesus, and the church he builds on the apostles — the trunk of everything on this page.

nodes.name: Rabbinic Judaism
nodes.blurb: After the Temple's destruction, Judaism is rebuilt around Torah, synagogue and the rabbis — Christianity's elder sibling, not its child.

nodes.name: The Early Church
nodes.blurb: From Jerusalem to the whole empire in three centuries — through persecution, the writing of the New Testament, and the church fathers.

nodes.name: Edict of Milan
nodes.blurb: Constantine and Licinius grant Christians the freedom to worship, ending three centuries of intermittent persecution. Within a dozen years an emperor is summoning the church's first general council — the faith has moved from the catacombs to the council chamber, for good and for ill.

nodes.name: Nicene Christianity
nodes.blurb: The councils of Nicaea and Constantinople confess Christ as fully God — the creed nearly every church on this page still holds.

nodes.name: Council of Chalcedon
nodes.blurb: Chalcedon confessed Christ in two natures and one person, and its canons ranked the great sees. Egypt, Syria and Armenia heard 'two natures' as dividing Christ himself and could not sign — so the church came out of 451 as two families instead of one.

nodes.name: The Five Patriarchates
nodes.blurb: Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem — the five great sees of the ancient church, from which the oldest branches descend.

nodes.name: Gnostic Movements
nodes.blurb: Teachers like Valentinus and Basilides offered salvation by secret knowledge, with the world's Maker a lesser god and Christ's flesh an appearance. Answering them pressed the church to say out loud what it had always assumed: one God who made matter and called it good, one Christ truly in the flesh, and a faith taught publicly, not whispered.

nodes.name: Marcion of Sinope
nodes.blurb: Marcion held that the God of Israel and the Father of Jesus were two different Gods, threw out the Old Testament entirely, and kept an edited Luke with ten of Paul's letters — the first list anyone is known to have drawn up. Rome expelled him and gave his money back. His truncated Bible is a large part of why the church set about naming its own.

nodes.name: Montanism (the New Prophecy)
nodes.blurb: A prophetic renewal out of Phrygia — Montanus with the prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla — calling for rigorous fasting, readiness for martyrdom and fresh utterance of the Spirit. It won Tertullian, the age's sharpest Latin mind, and raised a question the church has never finally closed: how does living prophecy sit under settled Scripture?

nodes.name: Arianism
nodes.blurb: Arius of Alexandria taught that the Son was the Father's first and highest creature — exalted, but not God as the Father is God. Nicaea condemned it in 325, yet for most of that century it held the imperial court, and the Germanic peoples evangelized in that window — Goths, Vandals, Burgundians, Lombards — carried it into the kingdoms they built on Rome's ruins. It outlived the empire by two centuries and then died with those kingdoms: the last Arian rulers conformed in the 580s to 660s, and by the late 7th century it was gone. The Nicene Creed exists because of this argument.

nodes.name: Donatists
nodes.blurb: When persecution ended, North African rigorists refused the ministry of bishops who had handed over the Scriptures under threat — a church of the pure, or none at all. Against them Augustine argued that a sacrament's worth rests on Christ, not on the minister's record. The Donatist church outnumbered his in Africa for a century.

nodes.name: Council of Ephesus
nodes.blurb: The council deposed Nestorius over how to name Christ's two natures in one person. The churches of the Persian Empire — outside Roman politics, and reading the Greek terms differently — never accepted it. The first lasting division in Christian history.

nodes.name: Church of the East
nodes.authority: Scripture read with the Antiochene fathers, and the first two ecumenical councils — Nicaea and Constantinople — under its own patriarch-catholicos.
distinctives: Two natures and two hypostases in one Christ
Prefers 'Mother of Christ' to 'Mother of God'
East Syriac liturgy — the Qurbana of Addai and Mari
Missionary from the start: India, Central Asia, China
nodes.blurb: The church of the Persian Empire, out of communion after the Council of Ephesus; often called 'Nestorian', though it rejects the label. Its missionaries reached China by 635.

nodes.name: St Thomas Christians (India)
nodes.blurb: India's ancient Christians trace their founding to the apostle Thomas; for centuries they worshipped in fellowship with the Church of the East.

nodes.name: Assyrian Church of the East
nodes.blurb: The continuing Church of the East, its patriarchate today in Erbil, Iraq — a small, ancient communion scattered by a century of persecution.

nodes.name: Ancient Church of the East
nodes.blurb: A 1968 division within the Assyrian church, largely over the calendar; based in Baghdad.

nodes.name: Oriental Orthodoxy
nodes.authority: Scripture within holy tradition, settled by the first three ecumenical councils — Nicaea, Constantinople and Ephesus — and by Cyril of Alexandria above all.
distinctives: Miaphysite: one united divine-human nature, 'out of two natures'
Does not receive Chalcedon or the councils after it
A communion of self-governing patriarchates, with no single head
Ancient fasting, and the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ge'ez rites
nodes.blurb: The churches that could not accept Chalcedon's wording about Christ's two natures — 'miaphysite', confessing one united divine-human nature. Their objection was never only theological: Chalcedon's canons also raised Constantinople to rank beside Rome, and Alexandria and Antioch — the sees being demoted — heard the imperial capital legislating over churches older than itself.

nodes.name: Coptic Orthodox Church
nodes.blurb: Egypt's ancient church, tracing its founding to Mark the evangelist in Alexandria; the mother church of African Christianity.

nodes.name: Syriac Orthodox Church
nodes.blurb: The church of Antioch's Syriac-speaking heartland, still praying in a dialect of the language Jesus spoke.

nodes.name: Armenian Apostolic Church
nodes.blurb: Armenia became the first Christian kingdom in 301; its church later stood with the non-Chalcedonian family.

nodes.name: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo
nodes.blurb: Founded under Frumentius and the kings of Aksum; daughter of the Coptic church until full independence in 1959, and Africa's largest ancient church.

nodes.name: Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo
nodes.blurb: Became a self-governing church after Eritrean independence, with the Coptic pope's blessing.

nodes.name: Coonan Cross Oath
nodes.blurb: Gathered at Mattancherry, the St Thomas Christians swore never again to submit to Portuguese bishops. The oath split India’s ancient church: a minority stayed with Rome, while most sought bishops from the Syriac Orthodox instead.

nodes.name: Malankara (Indian) Orthodox
nodes.blurb: After the Coonan Cross Oath against Portuguese control, many St Thomas Christians aligned with the Syriac Orthodox — India's Oriental Orthodox family.

nodes.name: The Great Schism
nodes.blurb: Legates from Rome and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated one another in 1054 — the formal rupture in a drift already centuries old, over papal authority, a clause added to the creed, and two halves of Christendom that had stopped listening to each other. East and West have been separate communions ever since.

nodes.name: Eastern Orthodox Church
nodes.authority: Scripture read inside Holy Tradition and settled by the seven ecumenical councils — never by one bishop over the whole church.
distinctives: Theosis — salvation as being made partakers of the divine nature
Rejects the Filioque: the Spirit proceeds from the Father
Icons venerated, as the seventh council defined
Conciliar government: a communion of equal self-governing churches
nodes.blurb: The Greek East after the schism: the Chalcedonian churches of Constantinople and the Slavic lands, holding the seven councils, governed as a communion of equals rather than under one see.

nodes.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate
nodes.blurb: Constantinople's patriarch, 'first among equals' of the Orthodox world — a seniority of honour, not a papacy.

nodes.name: Georgian Orthodox Church
nodes.blurb: Georgia's national church, evangelized by St Nino in the 320s; its independence was suppressed under Russia and restored in 1917.

nodes.name: Antiochian Orthodox Church
nodes.blurb: The Chalcedonian half of the ancient patriarchate of Antioch — the city where believers were first called Christians. Arabic-speaking, seated today in Damascus, and with a large diaspora in the Americas that has drawn in many Western converts.

nodes.name: Bulgarian Orthodox Church
nodes.blurb: The first Slavic national church to win its own patriarchate, in 927 — fruit of the mission of Cyril and Methodius's disciples.

nodes.name: Russian Orthodox Church
nodes.blurb: Prince Vladimir's baptism of Kyiv in 988 planted the faith among the Rus; Moscow became a patriarchate in 1589 — the largest Orthodox church.

nodes.name: Serbian Orthodox Church
nodes.blurb: St Sava won self-government for the Serbian church in 1219; it remains at the heart of Serbian identity.

nodes.name: Nikon’s Service-Book Reforms
nodes.blurb: Patriarch Nikon corrected Russian service books and even the sign of the cross against contemporary Greek models. To many believers the changes touched holiness itself rather than detail; the councils of 1666–67 anathematized all who refused, and Russian Orthodoxy tore in two.

nodes.name: Old Believers
nodes.blurb: Russians who refused Patriarch Nikon's revisions to the service books, and were fiercely persecuted for keeping the old rites.

nodes.name: Church of Greece
nodes.blurb: Independent after the Greek War of Independence — the national church of the modern Greek state.

nodes.name: Romanian Orthodox Church
nodes.blurb: United and self-governing from 1872, a patriarchate from 1925 — today the second-largest Orthodox church.

nodes.name: Orthodox Church in America
nodes.blurb: Grown from the Russian mission to Alaska (1794), granted self-rule by Moscow in 1970.

nodes.name: Orthodox Church of Ukraine
nodes.blurb: Recognized by Constantinople in 2019 as Ukraine's self-governing church — a recognition Moscow rejects; the wound is still open.

nodes.name: Roman Catholic Church
nodes.authority: Scripture and Tradition together, interpreted by the living magisterium of the bishops in communion with — and under — the pope.
distinctives: Papal primacy, and since 1870 papal infallibility
Seven sacraments
Transubstantiation: the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood
Purgatory, and the intercession of Mary and the saints
nodes.blurb: The Latin West under the bishop of Rome — through the medieval centuries, the Counter-Reformation, and two Vatican councils, the largest body in Christianity.

nodes.name: Eastern Catholic Churches
nodes.blurb: Twenty-three Eastern churches in full communion with Rome while keeping their own rites — Maronite, Chaldean, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Melkite, Syro-Malabar and more.

nodes.name: Council of Trent
nodes.blurb: Rome's own reforming council answered the Reformation point by point — defining canon, tradition, justification and the sacraments, and ending abuses that had helped provoke the split. It also set the divide in stone: the two Wests were now confessionally, not merely politically, apart. Its settlement shaped Catholic life for four centuries.

nodes.name: Second Vatican Council
nodes.blurb: Rome opened the windows: the liturgy in the people's own languages, Scripture put into every hand, and a warmer word for other Christians. Most Catholics received it gladly — a minority held that the council had given away exactly what Trent was called to defend.

nodes.name: Traditionalist movements (SSPX)
nodes.blurb: After Vatican II, Archbishop Lefebvre's Society of St Pius X kept the old Latin Mass; its standing with Rome remains irregular.

nodes.name: Benedictine Monasticism
nodes.blurb: Benedict's Rule — prayer and work, under an abbot, in one place for life — became the pattern for Western monasticism. For centuries the monasteries were the West's schools, hospitals, farms and copyists: nearly every ancient book we still have survived because a monk wrote it out again.

nodes.name: Friars — Franciscans & Dominicans
nodes.blurb: A new kind of order that owned nothing and stayed nowhere: Francis's brothers preaching poverty in the growing towns, Dominic's preaching against heresy with study as their weapon. Between them they put the church back on the road — and gave the medieval universities their finest teachers, Aquinas among them.

nodes.name: Society of Jesus (Jesuits)
nodes.blurb: Ignatius of Loyola's company, approved in 1540 under a special vow of obedience to the pope — schoolmasters, spiritual directors and missionaries who went wherever they were sent. They were the sharp edge of the Catholic Reformation, and carried it to India, Japan, China and the Americas.

nodes.name: First Vatican Council
nodes.blurb: The council defined papal infallibility: the pope, teaching solemnly from his office on faith and morals, is preserved from error. It settled centuries of argument about where authority finally rests in the Western church — and a body of German, Swiss and Dutch scholars who could not accept it walked out.

nodes.name: Old Catholic Churches
nodes.blurb: Those who rejected the 1870 definition, joined by the long-independent see of Utrecht, formed their own communion in 1889 — Catholic in worship and orders, without the papacy. Small, and in full communion with the Anglicans since 1931.

nodes.name: Waldensians
nodes.blurb: Peter Waldo of Lyon gave away his wealth and sent out lay preachers with a vernacular Bible — persecuted for centuries, and still alive in Italy today.

nodes.name: Wycliffe & the Lollards
nodes.blurb: John Wycliffe's circle translated the first complete English Bible and questioned the church's wealth and hierarchy — 'the morning star of the Reformation'.

nodes.name: Jan Hus & the Hussites
nodes.blurb: The Bohemian reformer, burned at Constance in 1415; his followers defied crusades and kept a reformed church in Bohemia a century before Luther.

nodes.name: Moravian Church
nodes.blurb: The Unity of the Brethren, renewed at Herrnhut in 1727 — pioneers of Protestant world mission whose warmth helped light John Wesley's heart.

nodes.name: The Reformation
nodes.blurb: Luther's Ninety-five Theses open a recovery of the gospel — salvation by grace alone through faith alone, and the Bible in the people's tongue. Every Protestant branch below descends from here.

nodes.name: Diet of Worms
nodes.blurb: Ordered to recant before the emperor, Luther refused and was declared an outlaw. Sheltered by his own prince, he spent the exile translating the New Testament into German — and the princes who protected him began reforming the churches of their own territories.

nodes.name: Lutheran State Churches
nodes.authority: Scripture alone — sola scriptura — confessed in the creeds and the Book of Concord, which is held to be a true reading of Scripture rather than a second source.
distinctives: Justification by grace alone through faith alone
Law and gospel rightly distinguished
Sacramental union: Christ truly present in, with and under the bread and wine
Infant baptism kept; bishops optional, the gospel is not
nodes.blurb: Germany and all Scandinavia adopt the Lutheran confession — Sweden 1527, Denmark and Norway 1536 — folk churches that carried the faith for centuries.

nodes.name: Pietism
nodes.blurb: Philipp Spener's Pia Desideria asked what a state church full of baptized strangers was for, and answered with small groups over the Bible, a living new birth, and lay people doing the work of ministry. Halle sent out the first Protestant missionaries. Nearly every warm-hearted movement below — Moravian, Methodist, Brethren, and the evangelicalism that came of them — drinks from this well.

nodes.name: Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod
nodes.blurb: Confessional German emigrants in America, holding firmly to the Book of Concord and the inerrancy of Scripture.

nodes.name: Evangelical Lutheran Church in America
nodes.blurb: The 1988 merger of America's larger Lutheran bodies — the mainline branch of US Lutheranism.

nodes.name: Reformed Churches
nodes.authority: Scripture alone, read covenantally and confessed in the Reformed standards — Heidelberg, Belgic, Westminster — which bind only as they are drawn from Scripture.
distinctives: The absolute sovereignty of God over all things
Election and predestination
Covenant theology binding the Testaments into one story
Government by elders — presbyters — in graded assemblies
Worship shaped only by what Scripture positively commands
nodes.blurb: Zwingli in Zurich and Calvin in Geneva build the Reformation's second great stream — God's sovereignty, covenant, and churches governed by elders.

nodes.name: French Huguenots
nodes.blurb: France's Reformed church, organized in 1559 and refined by fire — massacre and exile scattered Huguenot believers (and their skills) across the world, including the Cape.

nodes.name: Dutch Reformed Church
nodes.blurb: The Reformed church of the Netherlands, whose Synod of Dort (1618–19) gave the classic five points of Calvinism.

nodes.name: Synod of Dort
nodes.blurb: Called to settle whether grace is finally God's choice or man's, the synod answered Arminius's followers point for point — the five heads of doctrine later remembered as the five points of Calvinism. It also ordered the Dutch Bible that shaped the language. The losing side was deposed and exiled, and Reformed Christianity has argued along this line ever since.

nodes.name: Arminians (Remonstrants)
nodes.blurb: Followers of Jacobus Arminius who petitioned in 1610 for a gentler reading of election — grace that can be resisted, an atonement offered to all. Condemned at Dort and driven out, they organized as their own church in 1619. Their theology outlived their numbers: Wesley preached it, and most of the Methodist and Pentecostal world holds it still.

nodes.name: NG Kerk (Dutch Reformed, South Africa)
nodes.blurb: Planted at the Cape with Van Riebeeck's settlement (first congregation 1665) — for three centuries the largest church of the Afrikaans world.

nodes.name: Church of Scotland (Presbyterians)
nodes.blurb: John Knox brings Geneva's reformation home; Scotland's kirk, governed by elders and courts, becomes the mother of world Presbyterianism.

nodes.name: Congregationalists (Puritans)
nodes.blurb: English Puritans who gathered self-governing congregations of the converted; the Mayflower Pilgrims carried the pattern to New England in 1620.

nodes.name: American Presbyterians
nodes.blurb: The first American presbytery met in Philadelphia in 1706; today's PC(USA) descends from a long line of unions.

nodes.name: Presbyterian Church in America
nodes.blurb: A conservative continuing church formed in 1973, holding the Westminster Standards and the inerrancy of Scripture.

nodes.name: United Church of Christ
nodes.blurb: The 1957 union that gathered America's Congregational and Evangelical-and-Reformed churches into one mainline body.

nodes.name: Operation Reformation
nodes.blurb: Nearly every conservative movement on this page ends the same way — a new denomination, and the old buildings left behind: the PCA in 1973, the ACNA in 2009. Operation Reformation, begun online around 2023 by the Presbyterian commentator known as Redeemed Zoomer, argues for the opposite move. Stay in the mainline churches your grandparents built, join their seminaries, presbyteries and conventions, and win them back from the inside — a reconquest, as its own supporters like to call it, rather than another exodus. Its named targets are the PC(USA), the United Methodist Church, the Episcopal Church and the ELCA. It is the youngest thing on this tree, and it is still an argument rather than a branch — whether it ever becomes one is genuinely undecided.

nodes.name: Act of Supremacy
nodes.blurb: Parliament declared Henry VIII supreme head of the church in England, settling a king's marriage dispute by cutting a whole realm loose from Rome. It began as a question of jurisdiction, not doctrine — but the door it opened is the one Cranmer's Prayer Book and Elizabeth's settlement walked through.

nodes.name: Church of England
nodes.authority: Scripture supreme, read with the tradition of the ancient church and with reason — the three-legged stool — as the Articles and the Prayer Book set it out.
distinctives: A via media holding catholic order and reformed doctrine together
Bishops in historic succession
The Book of Common Prayer as the shape of belief
Comprehension: high, low and broad churchmanship under one roof
nodes.blurb: Henry VIII's break with Rome became, under Cranmer and Elizabeth, a reformed church with an ancient shape — Bible, Prayer Book, bishops.

nodes.name: Elizabethan Settlement
nodes.blurb: Elizabeth's Act of Uniformity fixed one Prayer Book and one church for England, framed broadly enough to hold most of the nation. Puritans who wanted the reform carried further stayed and pressed for it; those who gave up on the established church left it altogether — and English free-church Christianity begins there.

nodes.name: English Separatists
nodes.blurb: Those who despaired of reforming the established church from within and left it — the seedbed of Baptists, Congregationalists and Quakers.

nodes.name: Episcopal Church (USA)
nodes.blurb: American Anglicans reorganized after independence — the first self-governing church of what became the Anglican Communion.

nodes.name: The Oxford Movement
nodes.blurb: Newman, Keble and Pusey argued that the Church of England was no creature of Parliament but a branch of the ancient catholic church, and set about recovering what went with that — the sacraments, the fathers, the religious orders, ceremony. It remade Anglican worship, sent slum priests into the cities, and lost Newman himself to Rome.

nodes.name: The Anglican Communion
nodes.blurb: The worldwide family of Anglican churches, meeting since the first Lambeth Conference of 1867; its centre of gravity is now the global South.

nodes.name: Anglican Church in North America
nodes.blurb: Formed in 2009 by conservatives leaving the Episcopal Church, recognized by many global-South Anglican provinces.

nodes.name: Anabaptists
nodes.authority: Scripture alone, read and applied together by the gathered congregation — with the plain words of Jesus, and the Sermon on the Mount above all, governing the rest.
distinctives: Believers' baptism only — infant baptism is no baptism
Church and state wholly separate; no oaths, no magistracy
Nonresistance and pacifism
A visible, disciplined community of disciples
nodes.blurb: Zurich radicals who baptized one another as believing adults in 1525 — the 'radical reformation' of gathered, non-violent, suffering churches.

nodes.name: Hutterites
nodes.blurb: Anabaptists who hold all goods in common, after Acts 2 — still living communally on the North American plains.

nodes.name: Mennonites
nodes.blurb: Named for Menno Simons, the Dutch priest who gathered the scattered Anabaptists into enduring peaceful churches.

nodes.name: Amish
nodes.blurb: Jakob Ammann's stricter Mennonites — plain dress, plain living, and community set apart from the modern world.

nodes.name: Brethren (Schwarzenau)
nodes.blurb: German Pietists baptized in the river Eder in 1708, blending Anabaptist and Pietist streams — ancestors of the Church of the Brethren.

nodes.name: Quakers (Society of Friends)
nodes.blurb: George Fox's movement of the Inward Light — silent waiting on God, plain speech, and early witness against slavery.

nodes.name: Baptists
nodes.authority: Scripture alone, with every local congregation free to read and order itself under Christ — no bishop, synod or convention over it.
distinctives: Believers' baptism by full immersion
Congregational autonomy
A regenerate church membership
Soul liberty and religious freedom for all, including dissenters
nodes.blurb: John Smyth's exiled English congregation embraced believers' baptism in Amsterdam in 1609; General (free-will) and Particular (Reformed) streams soon grew.

nodes.name: Particular Baptists
nodes.blurb: London's Calvinistic Baptists, whose 1689 confession still anchors Reformed Baptist churches — the stream of Bunyan, Carey and Spurgeon.

nodes.name: Southern Baptist Convention
nodes.blurb: Formed in 1845 in a split over slavery (a beginning it has formally repented of); today the largest Protestant denomination in the United States.

nodes.name: National Baptist Conventions
nodes.blurb: The great Black Baptist conventions, gathered in 1895 — the churches that carried, and led, the American civil-rights movement.

nodes.name: American Baptist Churches USA
nodes.blurb: The northern Baptist family, organized nationally in 1907 — the tradition of Roger Williams and the first Baptist church in America (1638).

nodes.name: Methodism
nodes.authority: Scripture first and finally, read with tradition, reason and living experience — the quadrilateral later named for Wesley.
distinctives: Free grace for all, not for the elect only
Assurance — the Spirit witnessing with our spirit
Sanctification, pressed on towards Christian perfection
Societies, class meetings and preaching in the open air
nodes.blurb: John Wesley's heart 'strangely warmed' in 1738; with Charles's hymns and field preaching, a revival society inside the Church of England became a worldwide church.

nodes.name: Methodist Episcopal Church
nodes.blurb: At the Christmas Conference in Baltimore, American Methodism became a church of its own — and grew faster than the frontier.

nodes.name: African Methodist Episcopal Church
nodes.blurb: Richard Allen, once enslaved, led Black Methodists out of segregated pews into the first Black-led denomination in America.

nodes.name: The Salvation Army
nodes.blurb: William and Catherine Booth took Wesley's gospel to London's poorest streets — soup, soap and salvation, under a flag instead of a steeple.

nodes.name: Holiness Movement
nodes.blurb: A revival of Wesley's teaching on entire sanctification — camp meetings and new denominations seeking a deeper work of grace. The dry tinder Pentecostalism would set alight.

nodes.name: Church of the Nazarene
nodes.blurb: The largest Holiness denomination, united at Pilot Point, Texas in 1908.

nodes.name: Christian & Missionary Alliance
nodes.blurb: A. B. Simpson's missionary movement around the 'fourfold gospel' — Christ our Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer and Coming King.

nodes.name: United Methodist Church
nodes.blurb: The 1968 union of American Methodism's main branches; in 2022 the Global Methodist Church separated from it over sexuality and Scripture.

nodes.name: Second Great Awakening
nodes.blurb: Camp-meeting revival swept the American frontier — filling the Methodist and Baptist churches and birthing the restorationist movements below.

nodes.name: Stone-Campbell Movement
nodes.blurb: 'Christians only, no creed but Christ' — Barton Stone's and the Campbells' movements united in 1832 to restore simple New Testament church life.

nodes.name: Churches of Christ
nodes.blurb: The a cappella stream of the restoration movement, congregational to the core.

nodes.name: Disciples of Christ
nodes.blurb: The restoration movement's ecumenical stream, known for weekly communion at an open table.

nodes.name: Plymouth Brethren
nodes.blurb: Believers in Dublin began breaking bread with no clergy at all; J. N. Darby's teaching here shaped dispensationalism and much of evangelical prophecy belief.

nodes.name: Millerites
nodes.blurb: William Miller's movement expected Christ's return in 1844; the Great Disappointment scattered them — into several adventist bodies.

nodes.name: Seventh-day Adventist Church
nodes.authority: Scripture as the only rule of faith, with Ellen White's writings received as a continuing gift of prophecy that points back to it rather than standing beside it.
distinctives: The seventh day — Saturday — kept as the Sabbath
The investigative judgment, begun in heaven in 1844
Conditional immortality: no conscious state between death and resurrection
Health, temperance and the whole person
nodes.blurb: Organized in 1863 with Ellen White among its founders — Sabbath-keeping, health-minded, and now one of the most widespread Protestant bodies on earth.

nodes.name: Azusa Street Revival
nodes.blurb: Speaking in tongues at Topeka (1901) and then William Seymour's multiracial revival on Azusa Street (1906) — the spring from which world Pentecostalism flows.

nodes.name: Church of God in Christ
nodes.blurb: Bishop C. H. Mason's church embraced the Azusa revival in 1907 — the largest Pentecostal denomination in the United States.

nodes.name: Church of God (Cleveland, TN)
nodes.blurb: An Appalachian holiness fellowship (1886) that received Pentecost after Azusa — now a global movement.

nodes.name: Assemblies of God
nodes.blurb: Organized at Hot Springs, Arkansas in 1914; today the largest Pentecostal family in the world.

nodes.name: Foursquare Church
nodes.blurb: Aimee Semple McPherson's Angelus Temple and its worldwide offspring — Jesus the Saviour, Baptizer, Healer and Coming King.

nodes.name: Apostolic Faith Mission (South Africa)
nodes.blurb: Azusa's fire reached Johannesburg with John G. Lake in 1908 — South Africa's first Pentecostal church, and the AFM remains one of its largest.

nodes.name: Charismatic Movement
nodes.blurb: From 1960 the gifts of the Spirit crossed into the historic churches — Anglican, Catholic, Reformed — renewing worship far beyond Pentecostal denominations.

nodes.name: Calvary Chapel
nodes.blurb: Chuck Smith welcomed the barefoot Jesus People of the California coast — verse-by-verse teaching and casual worship that reshaped evangelicalism.

nodes.name: Vineyard Movement
nodes.blurb: John Wimber's 'signs and wonders' churches — intimate worship and everyday ministry in the Spirit's power; its songbook went round the world.

nodes.name: British New Church Movement
nodes.blurb: House churches seeking New Testament church life with present-day apostles and prophets — the stream of Terry Virgo's Newfrontiers and many church-planting families.

nodes.name: NCMI (New Covenant Ministries Int'l)
nodes.blurb: A South African-born apostolic team relating to local churches across the nations — part of the same restoration stream as Newfrontiers.

nodes.name: Four12 Global / Joshua Generation
nodes.blurb: Joshua Generation Church (Cape Town) grew into Four12 Global — a partnership of churches across several nations, contending for apostolic New Testament Christianity.

nodes.name: Non-denominational & Evangelical
nodes.authority: Scripture alone, under a local eldership answerable to no wider body — and in practice under whichever teachers a congregation trusts.
distinctives: The new birth as the thing that makes a Christian
The Bible as final in every question
The cross as the heart of the message
Activism: mission, evangelism and mercy as the normal Christian life
nodes.blurb: Independent Bible-centred congregations — from megachurches to house fellowships — now one of the largest 'families' in world Christianity, though they'd resist the label. A caution about this box: EVANGELICAL is not really a denomination at all but a movement running crossways through the tree, and there are evangelical Presbyterians, Anglicans, Baptists and Methodists who belong firmly to their own family and not to this one. What sits here is only the part of that movement that ended up unaffiliated.

nodes.name: African-Initiated Churches
nodes.blurb: Thousands of churches founded by African leaders — Ethiopian, Zionist and Apostolic streams — now numbering tens of millions across the continent.

nodes.name: Zion Christian Church
nodes.blurb: Engenas Lekganyane's church, headquartered at Moria in Limpopo — its Easter gathering is among the largest Christian assemblies anywhere.

nodes.name: Kimbanguist Church
nodes.blurb: Born from Simon Kimbangu's brief 1921 ministry in the Congo — he spent the rest of his life in a colonial prison; the church grew regardless.

nodes.name: Nazareth Baptist Church (Shembe)
nodes.blurb: Isaiah Shembe's church, gathered at Ekuphakameni in KwaZulu-Natal — Sabbath-keeping, barefoot before God, and worshipping in sacred dance. One of the largest African-Initiated churches in South Africa, and among the most distinctly Zulu in its forms.

nodes.name: Aladura Churches (Nigeria)
nodes.blurb: The 'owners of prayer' — Yoruba prayer movements born in the influenza years and the revival of 1930: the Cherubim and Seraphim, the Church of the Lord, the Christ Apostolic Church. Healing, prophecy and fasting instead of the mission hospital, and the seedbed of Nigeria's later Pentecostal explosion.

nodes.name: Redeemed Christian Church of God
nodes.blurb: Founded in Lagos in 1952, now planting churches on every continent — a flagship of Nigeria's extraordinary missionary energy.

nodes.name: Unitarian Universalism
nodes.blurb: New England Congregationalism's liberal wing set aside the Trinity; merged with the Universalists in 1961 into a creedless association.

nodes.name: Latter-day Saints (Mormons)
nodes.authority: Continuing revelation through a living prophet, with the Bible, the Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price as open scripture.
distinctives: A total apostasy of the early church, restored through Joseph Smith in 1830
Father, Son and Spirit as three distinct beings, one in purpose
Temple ordinances, including baptism for the dead
Eternal progression
nodes.blurb: Joseph Smith's restoration movement with new scripture (the Book of Mormon) and a distinct doctrine of God — outside Nicene Christianity by its own account and others'.

nodes.name: Christadelphians
nodes.blurb: John Thomas's Bible-study movement, rejecting the Trinity while awaiting Christ's literal kingdom.

nodes.name: Jehovah's Witnesses
nodes.authority: Scripture as read and taught by the Governing Body, in its own New World Translation.
distinctives: Rejects the Trinity: Jesus is God's first creation, the Spirit God's active force
Only Jehovah is properly God's name
144,000 reign in heaven; the rest hope for an earthly paradise
No blood transfusions, no military service, no national symbols
nodes.blurb: Charles Taze Russell's Bible Students, renamed in 1931 — door-to-door witness, a distinct New World Translation, and a non-Trinitarian theology.

nodes.name: Christian Science
nodes.blurb: Mary Baker Eddy's teaching that sickness is an error of mind to be healed by prayer — a 19th-century 'metaphysical' reading of Christianity.

nodes.name: Oneness Pentecostalism
nodes.blurb: The 'New Issue' that split early Pentecostalism — baptism in Jesus' name only and a rejection of the Trinity; today's United Pentecostal Church and related bodies.

perspectives.label: Catholic
perspectives.truechurch: The church Christ built on Peter, governed ever since by Peter's successors at Rome — never founded, never re-founded, only continued.
perspectives.others: Everyone else left. The Eastern churches are true churches with real bishops, real sacraments and a real apostolic descent, but out of communion; the churches of the Reformation are Christian communities that gave up the orders which would make them churches in the full sense. The road home is reunion, not reinvention.

perspectives.label: Eastern Orthodox
perspectives.truechurch: The undivided church of the seven councils, still praying and believing what it prayed and believed in 787 — because it never took the step that would have changed it.
perspectives.others: Rome was the one that moved: it added to the creed and then claimed a jurisdiction over the other patriarchs that the ancient church never gave anyone. Protestantism is the argument Rome's innovation eventually caused, and inherits the same wound at one further remove.

perspectives.label: Protestant
perspectives.truechurch: One church running the whole way through, sometimes buried under medieval accretion and sometimes visible, brought back into the light in the 16th century by the Word.
perspectives.others: The Reformation restored a church rather than starting one, so the fathers, the creeds and the councils are Protestant inheritance and not foreign property. Rome and the East are true churches carrying real corruption; the question is not who is older but who is now standing on Scripture.

perspectives.label: Anglican — branch theory
perspectives.held: Anglicans of the high-church and Oxford Movement stream
perspectives.truechurch: No single body. One church, growing in three great branches — Rome, the East and the churches with bishops in historic succession — each holding the catholic faith, none holding all of it alone.
perspectives.others: The branches are separated but not unchurched, and reunion is a matter of healing rather than of surrender. Never a majority position even inside Anglicanism, and firmly rejected by both the branches it most wants to embrace.

perspectives.label: Baptist — Trail of Blood
perspectives.held: Landmark Baptists and some independent Baptist churches
perspectives.truechurch: A thin line of small, persecuted, believer-baptizing congregations running unbroken from the apostles to now, mostly outside the record because the people writing the record were hunting them.
perspectives.others: The great institutional churches took a wrong turn once they were joined to the state, and the martyrs in every century are the real succession. Most Baptist historians today do not hold this — the medieval groups it claims are hard to line up with each other, let alone with modern Baptists — but the story has been powerfully told and is still believed.

perspectives.label: Restorationist
perspectives.held: Latter-day Saints, Jehovah's Witnesses and other restoration movements
perspectives.truechurch: None, for most of history. The apostles died, authority went with them, and what followed was an apostasy — until the church was restored in the 19th century.
perspectives.others: Every branch on this tree, East and West alike, is a record of that long absence rather than of a survival. This is the only view here that needs the centuries in between to have failed, and it is why these bodies sit outside the Nicene family on the chart rather than inside it.

perspectives.label: Religious studies — the outsider
perspectives.held: Historians writing as historians, whatever they believe on Sunday
perspectives.truechurch: Not a question this method can take. 'The true church' is a theological claim, and the discipline is built to describe what people believed and did, not to rule on whether they were right.
perspectives.others: Every branch is studied the same way — texts, politics, money, geography, who had the emperor's ear. That even-handedness is the method's strength and its limit: it can tell you exactly how a split happened and has nothing to say about which side should have won.
